articleBlocks: Albatross, Eagle, and Birdie can look like a bird board at first, especially because the first three clues all share that animal theme.
The puzzle becomes more precise once you notice those same words also live inside golf scoring language.
Par is the clue that really settles the board.
Once Par appears, Albatross, Eagle, and Birdie stop behaving like birds and start reading as scores relative to the golfing baseline.
Bogey (or worse) then confirms the full ladder by adding the score that falls above par instead of below it.
This board is elegant because it uses the order of the clues, not just the clue meanings, to show a progression from best result to worst.
fullAnalysis: Albatross, Eagle, and Birdie are all real golf terms, but the first three clues can still mislead you into thinking the puzzle is simply about birds.
That misread is part of what makes the board work, because bird names alone do not explain why the clues feel like they might belong together.
Par is the turning clue because it names the standard score in golf, which makes the sports context explicit and reinterprets the earlier clues immediately.
Once Par lands, Albatross, Eagle, and Birdie all become under-par results, while Bogey (or worse) becomes the over-par result that completes the scale.
The order matters too: the board moves from the rarest great result through the baseline and out to the weaker score on the other side.
solutionNarrative: The opening trio looked like birds first, which is exactly why the board holds back its answer. I could see a thematic set, but not yet a category tight enough for Pinpoint.
Par changed everything. Once the scoring benchmark appeared, the bird names became golf jargon instantly, and Bogey (or worse) finished the under-par to over-par progression.

lessons.title: Benchmark clues can beat thematic clues
